title: The Singing Reeds of Lumina
markdown:
Suri’s workroom was a snug corner of the academy, humming with small machines. Trays of cuttings lined the shelf above her bunk: a leaf that stored starlight, a vine that drank fog, a sample she had not yet named. The air smelled of stardust and the sharp green of strange plants. Tonight the space felt too small, a nest before hatching. The annual prize for alien flora was days away. Hal, another apprentice — quick mind, sharper tongue — had already plastered the halls with posters, each one a monument to careful columns. Suri was still listening to Lumina’s crystal reeds. Their secrets slipped like moonbeams through a fist.

She wanted, more than the prize, to prove that her way of working — following curiosity as much as protocol — was not a daydream. Teachers, wise and stuck in old maps, had questioned her “creative” methods in the kind of voices used for almost-failing. A quiet worry fluttered under her ribs, a mouse in a wall. What if the shimmering patterns she heard were only hers? What if she could never make anyone else see the quiet messages in those songs? Her hands shook a little as she adjusted Patch, her small round translator bot, a friend whose beeps and whirs were more comforting than most words. He blinked a green diode, which was his way of saying he was ready even when she was not.

“Alright, Patch.” She set fog-goggles on her face. The world went soft, a watercolor through wet glass. In the goggles’ first second she always thought of Earth rain on a greenhouse roof, then of Lumina, which had never agreed to be Earth. “Time to face the mist.”

Outside, Lumina’s fog was a living grey blanket that sanded the sharp edges off everything familiar. Cool damp on her cheeks. The reeds chimed, a music that sank into bone, notes that belonged to no Earth garden and to no lecture slide. This was the shimmering edge of the known, and the middle of her research.

She could see only a few steps. The reeds stood tall and thin, like frozen starlight given stems, their bell-tops swaying in air that barely moved, letting out haunting musical sighs. Suri fumbled the recording gear. Delicate sensors worked too hard, or not hard enough. She crouched, stood, crouched again, chasing layered phrases the way you chase a smell you almost remember. Every rustle, every change of pitch, was a piece. Patch hovered at her lip, logging, occasionally offering a beep that meant still here.

Hal’s voice cut through, ice in silk. “Still messing around, Suri? Some of us collect real information before the contest.”

Her stomach tightened. She noticed, even so, a change in the song: a deep humming chord that echoed a feeling from yesterday, the ache of her grandmother’s garden, damp soil and roses after rain. She tried it on Patch, who chirped encouraging questions.

“It’s like the smell of rain on flowers after a long dry spell,” she whispered.

Hal made a dismissive sound. “Coincidence. Air pressure. Ground shake. Not your sappy stories.”

A wave of pure sound washed over them, richer and stronger than anything in the logs. The world shimmered. Fog swirled into ghost shapes, dancers without feet. Suri felt a dizzy backward slide into a dream that did not owe her sense. Her feet seemed to grow roots into the misty ground. Her heart went uneven, a drum that had lost the count. The urge to turn back — to the warm dry academy, to Hal’s tidy posters, to a prize she might lose honestly — was almost enough. The fear said, quite clearly, you don’t belong here. She tasted metal. She stayed.

“Wait.” Her hand found her forehead. “It isn’t air pressure. It’s us.” She pointed at the nearest reed, which trembled with a private intensity. “When I thought of the garden, that reed sang one way. When you complained about your sensor, that patch sounded like annoyance.”

Patch translated her breathless rush into a burst of confirmations. The reeds were not only singing. They were listening. Memories. Feelings. The core of a person. Bigger than a prize.

Seeing it would not convince Hal, or the faculty. Proof meant offering a memory and letting the reeds answer. She chose one she rarely touched: saying goodbye to her childhood land-cat, also called Pip, fluff and dry grass and a small whimper in a bedroom she had outgrown. The ache was still sharp. Sharing it felt like stepping out of her own skin under Hal’s gaze. She nodded to Patch anyway.

She focused. Smell of dry grass underfoot. The almost invisible brush of Pip’s fur against her cheek. The tiny sad whimper that had lived in a small bedroom on another world. The details arrived whole. The nearby reeds leaned, as if courtesy were a kind of physics. Their chime changed — softer, sadder, a gentle lament. The air grew heavy, thick with a feeling that was no longer only hers. The sound pulsed, a low thrum through the soles of her boots. She stood in it, exposed on an alien plain, private grief broadcast across fog, and did not take the memory back. Hal, for once, did not speak. Patch’s diode went a quieter green.

They gathered notes with a space still between them, two methods that had not yet shaken hands. Hal’s columns. Her offered ache. The prize receded, a faint star behind weather she no longer trusted as the only explanation. Walking back, the fog thinned by degrees. Distant academy lights showed, ordinary and kind, a constellation someone had arranged on purpose.

In the workroom the stardust smell was a relief. Suri spread the traces on her screen and looked at them without hunting for a teacher’s nod. The moth-fear that had battered her ribs was only a breeze now, moving the leaves of something like confidence. She slept badly and woke clearer.

The next day Hal, practical as always, stood in the doorway and waved at a small change in the overnight song. “Weather,” he said. “Pressure drop. I checked the station log.”

Suri smiled. She did not argue him into her grandmother’s roses. She remembered the reeds’ soft sigh when she had offered Pip — a sadness that had warmed as it left her, like a blanket someone else had folded. She adjusted Patch’s tiny aerial, a click no louder than a reed’s bell, and let the recording run on without a caption. Outside, even through the wall, Lumina’s mist kept singing to whoever would bring it a true thing.
characters: Suri (apprentice xenobiologist), Hal (school rival), Patch (pocket translator bot)
